heading: Routes are nodes, not stops
body:
**Mind flip:** don't treat bus stops as graph nodes. Instead, **each route is a node**. Two routes connect if they share a stop.

Why? Each BFS level = one more bus boarded. You win when *any route at this level* contains your target stop.

heading: Build a stop → routes map
body:
The adjacency list maps each stop to all routes servicing it:
```python
bus_stops[stop] = [route_i, route_j, ...]
```
This lets you hop from one route to *all connected routes* by checking which other routes share any of its stops.

label: Crux · Python

q: Why do we treat bus routes (not stops) as graph nodes?
options: Because stops are harder to represent in code
Because each BFS level then represents taking one more bus, making the solution simpler
Because there are fewer routes than stops
Because we need to track which routes we've visited
explain: Treating routes as nodes means each edge traversal = boarding a new bus. BFS levels naturally count buses taken.
